transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m spending hours rechecking things—my dressing supplies, the door locks, file dimensions, revision notes. I don’t feel like I can move on until I’ve repeated the routine enough times for the anxiety to settle down.
What specific thoughts or fears go through your mind if you don't recheck those things?

Even when I’ve cleaned the wound area or checked a CAD file, I keep thinking I missed some tiny detail. Then I worry it could cause an infection or a design mistake that hurts somebody. I know I’ve looked, but I can’t seem to reason the thought away.
How long have you been dealing with these intrusive worries and checking routines?
I’m not really sure how long exactly. It’s been going on for a while, but I can’t pin down when it started.
Has this been happening almost every day for at least the past two weeks?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t kept track closely enough to say whether it’s been almost every day for the last two weeks.
Do you try to resist or stop yourself from performing these rechecking routines?

I do try to stop sometimes, but it’s hard. I feel like I’m not allowed to move on until I’ve checked the dressing supplies, locks, or work files enough times for the anxiety to settle down. And that can take a long time—hours, sometimes.
Do these intrusive thoughts feel like they come from your own mind, rather than being put there by an outside force?

Yes. I know they’re my own thoughts. It’s like even after I’ve cleaned a wound area or reviewed a CAD file, this thought cuts in that I missed one tiny thing and it could cause an infection or a mistake that hurts someone. I can’t just reason it away.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent, intrusive, distressing thoughts (fears of contamination, harm, or making critical errors) recognized as originating from their own mind (obsessions), accompanied by repetitive rechecking behaviors (compulsions) performed to neutralize anxiety. The symptoms cause notable distress and time consumption, fulfilling the core clinical picture of obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42).
